get.description: Carries `has_player_profile`, the fourth branch of onboarding's entry gate. It is read from the profile's event stream rather than from a projection, so a player who has just committed their profile is never sent back into the social steps by a read model that has not caught up.

post.summary: Authenticate and obtain an access/refresh token pair
Start an assessment and receive its opening question
post.description:
Idempotent per player and sport. Starting a sport that already has an unfinished run returns **that** run and its outstanding question with a 200, rather than opening a second one — so a double-tapped confirm, or a retry after a lost response, costs nothing. A sport whose previous run was abandoned still starts a new run, with a 201.

Both outcomes carry the same body, so a client that only routes on the step needs no branch; the status code is there for one that wants to tell the two apart.

**A sport this player is already rated at is refused with a 409** (`sport_already_rated`). A rating stream is keyed by player and sport and initialisation is its only transition, so a second completed run for one sport cannot be stored — and refusing at the start is the only point at which refusing costs the player nothing rather than a whole questionnaire. The picker offers unrated sports, so no shipped flow reaches this.

201.description: A new assessment was started; its opening question is returned.

200.description: An assessment for this sport was already in progress; its outstanding question is returned and nothing was created.

409.description: `sport_already_rated` — this player already holds a Skill rating for this sport, so no assessment is started.

get.summary: Resume: one sport's in-progress assessment, or every sport's
get.description:
One question — *which of this player's runs are unfinished* — asked two ways.

**With `sport`,** the answer is that sport's outstanding run as an `AssessmentStepResponse`, carrying its outstanding question, or a 204 when there is none. This is the resume read, unchanged.

**Without `sport`,** the answer is an `InProgressAssessmentsResponse`: every unfinished run this player holds, at most one per sport, ordered by the sport registry, and an empty list — with a 200, never a 204 or a 404 — when there are none. Each entry carries the assessment id and its sport, which is what a router needs; it carries no question, because the caller re-reads the run it routes to and the empty answer is the common one.

Which shape comes back is decided by the parameter, so a caller that always omits `sport` always sees the collection.

schema.title: Response Find In Progress Api V1 Assessments In Progress Get

204.description: No assessment in progress for that sport. Only ever returned when `sport` is supplied.

get.summary: Fetch an assessment's current state — its question or its result

post.summary: Finish a stopped assessment: create its Skill rating
post.description:
**The irreversible one.** The questionnaire *stopping* and the assessment *completing* are two moments: answering the question that stops the run creates nothing and leaves every answer revisable, and this request is what turns those answers into a Skill rating. So a client can show the whole set of answers back to the player, still changeable, before anything is committed.

Callable only on a **stopped** run — one whose step carries neither a `question` nor a `result` while `status` is still `in_progress`. A run with a question outstanding, and one that was abandoned, are both refused with `assessment_not_stopped`.

The finished step comes back inline, `result` and all, because the player is shown their rating on the very next screen. **Calling it twice is safe**: the second call records nothing and returns the same result, so a double-tapped submit produces one rating rather than a conflict the client has to translate.

Once this has been called the run's answers are settled: a change is refused with `answer_not_revisable`.

409.description: `assessment_not_stopped` — the questionnaire has not finished asking, or the run was abandoned. Refetch the current step and render it.

post.summary: Abandon an in-progress assessment, freeing the sport to start again
Answer the outstanding question, or change an answer already given
post.description:
**One request, decided by what the run has already answered.**

- A `question_id` the run has *not* answered must be the outstanding one: this is an ordinary answer, and the next question comes back — or **no question at all**, which is the questionnaire stopping.
- A `question_id` the run *has* answered with a **different** `option_id` is a **revision**. The answers given after it are discarded, because each was pitched at a difficulty chosen from the estimate as it then stood, and the response is whatever the questionnaire asks next given the shortened set of answers. That may be a question, and it may be the stop — changing the opening answer to *I have never played* ends the questioning there.
- A `question_id` the run has answered with the **same** `option_id` records nothing and returns the current step. So a retry after a lost response is free, and so is changing your mind and changing it back.

**`question` and `result` both null, with `status` still `in_progress`, is the stop.** No further question would meaningfully tighten the estimate, and nothing has been rated: the run waits, with every answer still revisable, until `POST /completion` is called. Answering never creates a Skill rating, so a client need not — and cannot — predict which question is the last one.

The `transcript` on every response is the answers as they now stand; after a revision it is **shorter**, and a client showing the run's progress should read it rather than remember what it last drew.

**Answers are revisable for as long as the run is, and no longer.** Once the run has produced a Skill rating, a change is refused with `answer_not_revisable` — a code of its own, because the recovery is to show the rating rather than to re-render a question.

400.description: `invalid_answer_option` — the chosen option is not one that question offers.

409.description: `question_not_outstanding` — the question is neither the one awaiting a response nor one this run has answered; refetch the current step and re-render it. `answer_not_revisable` — this run's Skill rating already exists, so its answers are settled; show the rating instead.

get.summary: The Skill ratings this player holds, one per rated sport
The Social tag vocabulary and how many to pick, and the Search radius bounds
get.description:
Read-only, unauthenticated, no request body. Tag **ids** and their grouping cross the wire; the label a player reads is the client's own copy.

A tag id is permanent — it is persisted on profiles, so retiring a tag means dropping it from this response while continuing to honour it on the profiles that hold it. Ids are never reused and never renamed.

Both the group order and the tag order within a group are part of the contract: the picker renders what it is given rather than sorting.

`social_tag_selection` carries how many tags a profile must hold — both ends included. The profile commit re-validates against the same numbers, so a picker that reads them here cannot disagree with it.

post.summary: Commit every answer from onboarding's second part
post.description:
Idempotent per `Idempotency-Key`. The same key twice creates one profile and returns the same body — the second call answers 200 and records nothing.

**Every rule the picker enforced is re-validated here.** The tag vocabulary, the tag floor and ceiling and the radius bounds are all served by `GET /player-profile/options` so a client can build controls that cannot produce an illegal value — and a disabled button is not a validation. Photo ids are checked to exist *and* to belong to the caller.

**The availability grid is required**, at least one of its twenty-one cells. Silence about when a player usually plays is never scored as a zero, so it is asked for rather than guessed at. The minimum is exactly one and is not served — it is fixed, and a client holds it as a constant.

**The proposals opt-in has no default.** Send the player's actual answer; `null` is refused rather than treated as a no. The answer is recorded with the moment, the copy version shown and the surface, because consent is evidenced rather than asserted.

**`gender` is required and `gender_preference` is not.** The first is asked once, here, with `PREFER_NOT_TO_SAY` a first-class answer — there is no unanswered state to send, so a missing or unknown value is a 422 rather than a coded refusal. The second defaults to `ANY`, is durable, and gates **both directions**: narrowing it also hides this player from the side it excludes. Neither value ever comes back out of this API.

parameters.name: Idempotency-Key

schema.description: What the client calls this commit. Sending the same key again returns the profile the first call created, with a 200 — one profile, one consent answer, whatever a flaky connection does to the response.
schema.title: Idempotency-Key

parameters.description: What the client calls this commit. Sending the same key again returns the profile the first call created, with a 200 — one profile, one consent answer, whatever a flaky connection does to the response.

200.description: This idempotency key has already been committed; the profile the first call created is returned and nothing was recorded.

400.description:
`unknown_social_tag` — an id this platform does not serve; re-read `GET /player-profile/options`.

`social_tag_selection_out_of_bounds` — too few or too many tags for the served floor and ceiling.

`duplicate_social_tag` — the same tag id arrived twice.

`search_radius_out_of_bounds` — outside the served range, or off its step.

`availability_grid_empty` — nothing ticked on the week. At least one of the twenty-one cells; the minimum is exactly one and is not served.

`proposals_opt_in_not_answered` — the answer was `null`. Ask the question; do not send `false` on the player's behalf.

`too_many_photos` / `duplicate_photo` — the photo list is not one a profile may hold.

404.description: `photo_not_found` — a photo id that does not exist, or belongs to another player. The two answer the same way deliberately.

409.description:
`player_profile_already_exists` — this player has a profile and this is a **different** idempotency key, so it is a second commit rather than a retry of the first.

`concurrent_modification` — two commits for this player raced and this one lost. Retry: the retry replays the winner.

post.description:
One photo per request. The body is the raw image and `Content-Type` names its format; JPEG, PNG and HEIC/HEIF are accepted.

**What is stored is not what was sent.** Every image is decoded and re-encoded to JPEG with its long edge capped, which is how EXIF — and with it the GPS coordinates a phone writes into a photo — is removed reliably rather than best-effort.

The returned id is what a profile commit carries; a photo becomes part of a profile only when a commit names it. Uploaded photos that are never committed are intended to be swept, and that sweep is not running yet.

**Every upload is checked against the on-court rule, and `review` says what the check concluded.** It never refuses: a `flagged` photo is stored, answers `201` and is committed like any other, and the warning is the client's to word. A photo the check could not be run on answers `allowed` — the reviewer's own outage is not a reason to tell a player anything about their photograph.

get.summary: A signed URL for one of your photos
get.description:
Returns a short-lived signed URL rather than the bytes: the store serves the image directly, so a photo never crosses this API twice.

A photo id that does not exist and one belonging to another player both answer `photo_not_found`, deliberately — the alternative is an endpoint that confirms whether a stranger's id is real.

**`review` is always `null` here**, and that is not `allowed`: this route does not read what the store holds beside the bytes. The on-court check's verdict crosses on the upload, where a player has just chosen the photograph it is about.

post.description:
The two of you disappear from each other's view everywhere, immediately, silently, in **both** directions.

**Idempotent.** Blocking somebody already blocked records nothing and answers 204.

**No cap, no cooldown and no rate limit**, and none will be added.

**There is no reason field.** A reason belongs to a report, and this is not one.

**Neither side is notified**, in either direction, and no response in this API reveals a block to the blocked party.

**The record is directed and the effect is symmetric.** Your block of them and their block of you are independent: lifting yours never lifts theirs, and neither of you can discover which way one went.

**It is forward-looking.** It removes each of you from the other's future listings; it does not reach into anything already agreed.

204.description: The block stands. Also the answer when it already stood — blocking is idempotent and a second call records nothing.

400.description: `cannot_block_yourself` — the caller named themselves as the other party.

409.description: `concurrent_modification` — two blocks of this player raced and this one lost. Retry: the retry is the idempotent no-op.

delete.description:
Lifts **your** block of this player, immediately.

**It lifts one direction.** If they have also blocked you, that block stands and the two of you stay invisible to each other — and nothing here tells you so.

**Idempotent, and it never 404s.** Unblocking somebody you never blocked answers 204 and records nothing, because a different answer would be this API reporting on somebody else's state.

204.description: Your block of this player is lifted. Also the answer when there was nothing to lift — the two cases are deliberately indistinguishable.

post.description:
Returns a ranked shortlist of at most **twenty** people worth messaging, **unpaginated** — there is no page two, and past the last row there is an honest empty state.

**The breakdown ships with the search, not behind a tap.** Every term, its weight, its value, its contribution and the evidence it read ride on every row, because *Why 78?* has to open instantly.

**Send asks, never facts.** Your radius, grid, tags, rating, intent and gender preference are read from your profile at request time. There is no per-search radius input.

**Relaxation is offered, never applied.** When the shortlist comes back short the envelope carries `rung_offers` — your times, then your radius x1.5, then x2.0 — each with a **real** count from a genuine re-run and its own window. Taking one is a **new search citing this one**: post again with `offered_by_search_id` and `rung`. Your saved preferences stay yours, and **the quality floor is never relaxed**, so *nobody tonight* stays a real answer.

**Competitive and for fun select different weight vectors**, and the list visibly inverts between them.

**Deliberately not idempotent.** Two taps are two searches.

**Re-sorting costs no round trip:** `search.sorts_available` says which controls to draw, and a sort that would reorder nothing is not in it.

200.description: A ranked shortlist of at most twenty, each row carrying a Fit out of a hundred and the complete breakdown that produced it. **An empty list is also a 200** — the honest empty state is an answer, and the pool it came from is described either way.

403.description: `account_held` — this account is under a live hold.

409.description:
`sport_not_rated` — you hold no rating for this sport.

`play_intent_not_declared` — you have not said what kind of evening you are after for it.

`player_profile_not_committed` — there is no profile to read a radius, a grid or an area from.

`rung_offer_not_found` — you cited a rung no search of yours offered. The widening is read off the offer, never off the request, so an unknown citation is refused rather than run narrow and recorded as widened.

503.description: Four distinct codes at one status, so a client can tell a transient outage from a refusal about *you*: `matchmaking_unavailable`, `gate_data_unavailable`, `index_too_stale`, `search_not_recorded`.

get.description:
Returns a search you ran earlier, in **the same shape the `POST` returned it**, so *Why 78?* opens as fast a month later as it did on the day.

**The record is immutable; the gates are live.** Blocks, holds, account state and the mutual gender preference are re-evaluated at read time, and nothing is rewritten by doing so.

**A row those gates now exclude is stated as withheld** — it keeps its place in the list, carries no person, and does not say which gate fired. Branch on `withheld`.

**A searcher may read their own search and nobody else's.**

parameters.name: search_id

schema.description: The answer's identity, from the POST
schema.title: Search Id

parameters.description: The answer's identity, from the POST

200.description: The recorded answer, **plus live gate state**. The same schema the `POST` returned — not a fuller one and not a slimmer one — with any row the fail-closed gates no longer admit **stated as withheld** rather than quietly missing.

403.description: `account_held` — this account is under a live hold. The hold points both ways, and it points at old answers too.

404.description: `search_not_found` — no search of **yours** has that id. A search belonging to somebody else answers exactly as one that never existed.

503.description:
`gate_data_unavailable` — a fail-closed gate could not be re-evaluated, so the answer is refused rather than served unverified.

`matchmaking_unavailable` — there is no index in this process to read the other side of the gender gate from.

post.description:
Seats a four — you and three others — chosen together rather than one at a time, and returns **all three arrangements** with a forecast each.

**Every gate binds all six pairs.** A block, a gender preference and the level tolerance are checked between *every two* of the four, not just between you and each of them. That is stricter than a shortlist and it compounds: a four can be impossible where candidates are plentiful, and the honest answer is a partial line-up carrying `NO_ADMISSIBLE_COMBINATION`.

**A seat is never filled below the quality floor** to complete a four, a newcomer least of all. *Three of four* is a real answer.

**Swapping sides costs no round trip.** All three arrangements cross, each with `is_best` and `is_evenest` — two separate booleans, because they can differ, which happens precisely when the four's levels are near-equal and balance has nothing left to say.

**Send `locked_seats` to hand-seat people.** From that moment the engine optimises **for the group** and says so in `search.optimised_for`, because you may end up with a worse individual match than an empty court would have given you.

**A seated card shows the same number the shortlist showed.** Nothing is re-scored when somebody sits down.

200.description: A seated line-up, every arrangement with its own forecast, and one reason this four beat the runner-up. **A seat may be unfilled and this is still a 200** — the empty seat says why.

403.description: `account_held` — this account is under a live hold.

409.description:
`sport_not_rated` — you hold no rating for this sport.

`play_intent_not_declared` — you have not said what kind of evening you are after for it.

`player_profile_not_committed` — there is no profile to read a radius, a grid or an area from.

`rung_offer_not_found` — you cited a rung no search of yours offered.

`locked_seat_not_available` — somebody you seated by hand cannot be seated in this line-up. **Which one is deliberately not said.**

503.description: `matchmaking_unavailable`, `gate_data_unavailable`, `index_too_stale`, `search_not_recorded`. The second one covers the **pairwise block mask**: a four is never seated on a gate that could not be evaluated.

post.description:
Returns every arrangement of a four **you** put together, each with its own forecast — for the builder, where you swap somebody in and the number has to move.

**This creates no search and records nothing.** Six swaps are not six searches, and recording them as such would put a lie in the one table the product judges itself by. There is no `search_id` in the response and nothing to read back.

**Seats may be empty.** A side with one player is read as if the missing player matched the one already there; the forecast comes back `provisional` with its `assumption`, and the moment you fill the seat the number is **exactly** the same as the final one.

**It is bound to a search you ran.** Every player you name must have appeared in that search's returned rows.

**No forecast arithmetic belongs on the client.** Every figure the builder can show comes from here or from `/lineups`.

200.description: Every arrangement of the four you composed, each with its own forecast. **Provisional while a seat is empty**, and the provisional figure becomes exactly the final figure the moment the seat fills.

403.description: `account_held` — this account is under a live hold.

404.description: `search_not_found` — no search of yours showed all of those players. **One code for four cases**: the search does not exist, it is somebody else's, it was for another sport, or it never showed one of these people. Telling them apart would answer questions about strangers one probe at a time.

409.description: `sport_not_rated`, `play_intent_not_declared`, `player_profile_not_committed` — the same three the search route owes, for the same reason: a forecast puts **you** on the court.

503.description:
`gate_data_unavailable` — blocks and holds are re-read live and a gate that cannot be evaluated excludes.

`matchmaking_unavailable` — the engine raised.

get.description:
**Outgoing and mutuals only.** There is no inbox: a yes nobody has answered stays silent, in both directions, which is what makes saying yes low-stakes. You are never told that somebody declined you, and you are never shown who said yes to you unless you said it back.

**Every outgoing row carries its own `expires_at`**, so the screen can show what is still live without knowing the window.

**`outstanding` carries the count and the cap for every sport**, before you are near either — a cap you cannot see is a refusal you cannot predict. Render these; never hardcode the number.

200.description: Your outgoing yeses, the ones that came back, and where each sport stands against its cap.

503.description: `gate_data_unavailable` — the block set could not be evaluated, so the list is refused rather than served unverified.

post.description:
One tap, costing nothing — and it actually does something: you rise in that player's next search for this sport, **with the reason printed**, so the lift is never mistaken for a match.

**Nobody is notified.** A one-sided yes is silent and stays silent. It becomes visible only when the other person goes looking for a game.

**`search_id` is required.** It says which search surfaced this person — a yes citing a search that is unknown, that is somebody else's or that never showed them is refused, never recorded with an empty link.

**Idempotent.** Tapping again returns the same yes with the same expiry, at `200`.

**It lapses.** Every yes carries its own `expires_at`; when it passes the yes is simply gone, and that person may be dealt to you again. **Never compute the expiry yourself** — the window is ruleset configuration and does not cross the wire as a number.

201.description: The yes stands, and it is new. It lapses at `expires_at`, which was dated the moment it was created.

200.description: You had already said this. **Nothing was created and nothing was extended** — the yes comes back with the expiry it was born with.

409.description:
`origin_search_not_found` — no search of **yours** showed that player for that sport. The origin key is refused rather than linked as null.

`outstanding_interest_cap_reached` — you already have the most yeses in flight this sport allows. **Nothing of yours is shortened to make room**; wait, or one of them comes back. The count and the cap are on `GET /api/v1/interest`.

post.description:
Deals one batch of cards: one judgement at a time, no mode to pick and no setup.

**Send the sport and nothing else.** The deck reads your own declared Play intent for it — *no preference* still gives you a working deck — and no mode crosses the wire in either direction.

**A spent deal deals again.** Post again for a new deal with a new `search_id`; running out of cards is not running out of people, and only a fresh deal that comes back empty means the pool is thin.

**The order is the deck's variety**: people who already said *Let's play* to you, then the liveliest, then the rest. There is no re-sort — `sorts_available` is empty here, because a deck is one card at a time.

**No widening is offered.** `rung_offers` is `null` on a deal: the relaxation ladder belongs to the shortlist.

**Read it back** through `GET /api/v1/searches/{id}`, in this same shape.

200.description: One deal: an ordered batch of at most ten cards, sharing one `search_id`. **An empty deal is also a 200** — a fresh deal that came back with nothing is the honest empty state, and the pool it came from is described either way.

403.description: `account_held` — this account is under a live hold.

409.description:
`sport_not_rated` — you hold no rating for this sport.

`play_intent_not_declared` — the deck has no mode to read, so it reads your declaration; without one there is nothing at all to go on. **Answering *no preference* is an answer** and gives you a working deck.

`player_profile_not_committed` — there is no profile to read a radius, a grid or an area from.

503.description: `matchmaking_unavailable`, `gate_data_unavailable`, `index_too_stale`, `search_not_recorded` — four distinct codes at one status, so a client can tell a transient outage from a refusal about *you*.

post.description:
Keeps somebody out of **your deck** for a while, and reaches nothing else.

**It is not a block, and it never becomes one.** You will still find that person in a shortlist tomorrow if you change your mind; it never touches their deck, and passing twice buys exactly the same window as passing once. The control that removes a person from a person is `POST /api/v1/blocks`, and it is meant to be the heavier gesture.

**Nobody is told.** Not them, not you: no count, no list, no *show them again*.

**`search_id` is required** — it says which deal this card came from.

204.description: Recorded. **Nothing is returned, and nothing ever will be** — there is no route through which a pass reaches anybody, including you.

409.description: `origin_search_not_found` — no search of **yours** showed that player for that sport. The origin is refused rather than linked as null.

pairing_id.title: Pairing Id
pairing_id.description: Which of the arrangements, stable within one answer

is_current.title: Is Current
is_current.description: The one being drawn: the best on a line-up, and the seat order you sent on a forecast.

is_best.title: Is Best
is_best.description:
Best by the group objective. **The objective itself is never returned** — a second score you would have to trust is worse than none — so `group_reason` names what decided it instead.

**Omitted on every arrangement when no objective was computed**, rather than pointed at something else: a line-up with a seat still open, a singles line-up, and every forecast. There is nothing to be best *by* in any of them — no cross pairs, no seat delta, no mean over three Fits — and *Even it out* is then the only selection there is. Draw `is_evenest`.

is_evenest.title: Is Evenest
is_evenest.description: The closest game of the three — what *Even it out* selects. **A separate boolean from `is_best` because the two can differ**, which happens precisely when the four's levels are near-equal and balance has nothing left to say.

ArrangementSchema.title: ArrangementSchema
ArrangementSchema.description:
One way round, with its own forecast. **All of them cross.**

There are exactly three pairings of four people and the engine walks all
three to choose. Returning what it already knows costs nothing and makes
*Even it out* a **selection** rather than a calculation — every swap the
builder permits is one of these, so there is no arithmetic left for a client
to be tempted by.

seat_index.title: Seat Index
seat_index.description: Which seat, stable across all three arrangements: 0 is you, 1 is beside you, 2 and 3 are across the net.

player_id.title: Player Id
player_id.description: Who is in this seat. **Omitted on an open seat** — the top-level `seats` list says why that one is open.

ArrangementSeatSchema.title: ArrangementSeatSchema
ArrangementSeatSchema.description:
One seat within one arrangement: where it is, and who is in it.

`relationship` is **stated and never inferred from the side** — the whole
partner/opponent asymmetry hangs on it, and a client deriving it would be a
second implementation of a domain rule.

status.title: Status
status.description:
`in_progress`, `completed` or `abandoned` — and the field that says which of two things *neither a question nor a result* means.

- `in_progress` **with** a `question`: the questionnaire, awaiting that answer.
- `in_progress` with **neither**: the questionnaire has **stopped**. No remaining question would meaningfully tighten the estimate, and nothing has been rated — every answer is still revisable, and `POST /assessments/{assessment_id}/completion` is what creates the Skill rating.
- `completed`: the `result` is here and the answers are settled.
- `abandoned`: neither, and the run ended without a rating.

questions_asked.title: Questions Asked
questions_asked.description: How many of this run's questions have been answered. The outstanding `question` is **not** counted — it has been put to the player but not answered — so a question counter reads this plus one, and a fresh run reports 0. Replayed from the transcript on every read, which is what lets a resumed run report the position it is really at rather than restarting at 1. Once the run is over this is the same number `result.questions_asked` carries.

transcript.title: Transcript
transcript.description: Every answer given in this run so far, in the order they were given, each with the question it answered **as that question was asked** — so an answered question can be rendered from the response alone, by a client that was never shown it. Empty, never absent, on a run with no answers yet: a fresh run and a run whose answers are being withheld are not two readings of one payload. Grows by one entry per answer and is replayed from the stream on every read, so it survives a reinstall and a second device with nothing cached locally. Length is `questions_asked`; the outstanding `question` is not in it, because it has not been answered.

AssessmentStepResponse.title: AssessmentStepResponse
AssessmentStepResponse.description:
The server-driven step: at most one of `question` / `result` is set, and
`transcript` is everything already answered behind it. Neither means the run
is not asking and has not been rated — see `status`.

AtStakeSchema.title: AtStakeSchema
AtStakeSchema.description:
What a **counted** game against this opponent would do to your Level.

Filled by the backend, never by the matcher and never by the client. Omitted
in for-fun, where a counted result is meaningless rather than unavailable.

next_slot.description: The soonest cell both ticked, or null when there is none

AvailabilityOverlapEvidence.title: AvailabilityOverlapEvidence
AvailabilityOverlapEvidence.description:
How much of the searcher's week the candidate is free in.

The term is ``|shared| / |mine|`` and has **no constants at all** — the
denominator is the searcher's own ticked cells, which is what makes the
reading asymmetric and what makes it a fact about the pair.

Overlap is evidence a game can be *arranged*, never a proposed time, which is
why a candidate sharing no slot at all is still shown: the times rung exists
for exactly that pairing.

day.title: Day
day.description: ISO weekday — 1 is Monday, 7 is Sunday. The grid is Monday-first.

AvailabilitySlotResource.title: AvailabilitySlotResource
AvailabilitySlotResource.description:
One ticked cell of the availability grid.

Two named fields rather than the single joined code the event stream stores.
The stream's code is a *storage* encoding chosen so a replay folds strings;
this is a contract a client renders a grid from, and a client that had to
split ``"3:EVENING"`` would be parsing our persistence format.

player_id.title: Player Id
player_id.description: The player to block. The blocker is the authenticated caller and is never sent.

surface.description: Which screen the block was made from. Recorded as context; no rule reads it.

BlockPlayerRequest.title: BlockPlayerRequest
BlockPlayerRequest.description:
*Do not show me this person again.*

``surface`` is a closed set the client already holds — the four screens that
show one player to another — and it is validated here rather than by the
domain because there is no served vocabulary for a client to hold a stale
version of. Nothing branches on it.

**There is no reason field and there never will be.** A reason for a block
belongs to a Report, and a request shape is where one would be added first.

BlockSurface.title: BlockSurface
BlockSurface.description: The four surfaces of `search-telemetry.md` §2, as a block records them.

withheld.title: Withheld
withheld.description: Present only on a read-back, where it is always `false`: the fail-closed gates were re-evaluated and this row still stands. A row they no longer admit arrives as the withheld shape instead.

fit.title: Fit
fit.description: The printed number, out of a hundred, and the only one a player is asked to trust. It contains no Liveness.

distance_km.title: Distance Km
distance_km.description: Whole kilometres between the two coarse areas. **Promoted out of the distance evidence** so the *Closest* sort reads a field rather than reaching into a variant, and **omitted** rather than sent as zero when the distance term stood down — which is what lets a stood-down row sort last instead of first.

terms.title: Terms
terms.description: Every term that fired, **ranked by contribution** — the reasons, in the order the arithmetic puts them in. The cap is the client's.

degraded_terms.title: Degraded Terms
degraded_terms.description: The terms that stood down: the renormalisation basis. Without it a Fit is uninterpretable — a 78 built on four terms and a 78 built on seven are different readings of the same number.

liveness_reasons.title: Liveness Reasons
liveness_reasons.description: Why this person moved, ranked by how far. **Codes only** — there is no field here a Liveness number could be written to.

inclusion_reason.description: Why this person is in the list at all, when the reason is one the searcher is owed. **A union of one**: only an interest lift *admits* anybody, and the two reasons that merely reorder stay in the store — one reaches you as a liveness reason instead, and the other is a third party's unpopularity you are owed no version of. Omitted otherwise.

at_stake.description: Omitted in for fun, where a counted result is meaningless rather than unavailable, and omitted today in competitive because the result-update rule does not exist.

would_be_forecast.description: What this candidate would leave on court. Precomputed only when a line-up has exactly one seat open, so **omitted on every shortlist**.

CandidateSchema.title: CandidateSchema
CandidateSchema.description:
One row of the shortlist: the pairing, and the person.

Three field families have a **different author** from the rest and are
attached by the backend after the scorer returns — the card, the at-stake
block and the distance. None of them is a fact the scorer may see, and none
may be computed by the client.

On a read-back this row means *the live gates still admit this person*, and
it says so: ``withheld`` is ``false``, positively, rather than absent. A row
the gates no longer admit is a :class:`WithheldRowSchema` instead, and the
two are a union precisely so that **rendering a person the product has agreed
not to show is not a shape this contract can hold** (``docs/adr/0109``).

social_tag_ids.title: Social Tag Ids
social_tag_ids.description: The tag ids this player picked, as served by `GET /player-profile/options`. The count is re-checked against the served floor and ceiling, and an id this platform does not serve is refused with `unknown_social_tag`.

photo_ids.title: Photo Ids
photo_ids.description: Ids returned by `POST /photos`, in the order the player arranged them — the first is the one a player card shows. At most 3; an empty list is valid. Every id is checked to exist and to belong to this player.

availability.title: Availability
availability.description: The cells of the week this player ticked. **At least one of the twenty-one** — an empty list is refused with `availability_grid_empty`. The minimum is exactly one and is not served: it is fixed, so a client holds it as a constant. Repeated cells are collapsed, and the floor is counted after that.

search_radius_km.title: Search Radius Km
search_radius_km.description: Whole kilometres, re-checked against the range and step served by `GET /player-profile/options`.

gender.description: The player's own answer, asked once. Required — `PREFER_NOT_TO_SAY` is a first-class answer and is what a player who does not want to say sends; there is no way to send nothing. It matches only unconstrained searches, which costs its holder reach, and the client is what says so at the moment of asking.

gender_preference.description:
Who this player is willing to be matched with. Optional, and `ANY` when it is not sent.

**It is mutual and durable.** It governs what reaches this player as well as what this player sees, so narrowing it makes them invisible to the excluded side entirely — including to searchers who asked for anybody. The client must say so at the moment of setting; learning it from silence is not acceptable. A single search may narrow this further and nothing may widen past it.

CommitPlayerProfileRequest.title: CommitPlayerProfileRequest
CommitPlayerProfileRequest.description:
Every answer from onboarding's second part, in one body.

**Photos are the only field with a default**, because holding none is a
legitimate answer to *add some photos*. Everything else is something this
request must actually carry — a location, a radius, a tag selection, an
answer to the proposals question, and **a week with something ticked in it**
(``docs/adr/0102``).

The week's *floor* is not spelled here, and that is the same decision the tag
selection's is: an empty list passes this schema and is refused by the domain
with ``availability_grid_empty``, so the client gets a code it can branch on
and a recovery it can offer, rather than a 422 that can only say some field
somewhere was wrong.

ConcernSchema.title: ConcernSchema
ConcernSchema.description:
The engine's own statement that a term is genuinely weak.

Judged where the weights and the curves are, over **points forgone** rather
than over a raw value — a social vibe of 0.20 costs under four points of a
competitive match and nearly twenty of a friendly, and only one of those is
worth warning anybody about. A client thresholding a value would be that
judgement in TypeScript, written differently in every client.

**Ranked by the engine, capped by the client**: a card shows one, *Why 78?*
shows all of them.

ConfidenceReasonResponse.title: ConfidenceReasonResponse
ConfidenceReasonResponse.description: Why confidence landed where it did: a stable key and the sentence shown.

ConsentSurface.title: ConsentSurface
ConsentSurface.description:
Where a player was standing when they answered.

Two values, and both are reachable. ``ONBOARDING`` is the only one the commit
can record — the commit *is* the end of onboarding's second part. The profile
screen edits the same value later (``docs/adr/0089``), which is what
``PROFILE`` is for; the aggregate transition it uses exists, and the endpoint
that drives it does not yet.

DayPart.title: DayPart
DayPart.description:
The three parts of a day a player may tick.

Closed, and deliberately coarse. The product asks *when do you usually play*,
and an answer finer than this would be a schedule — which is the thing a
preference is explicitly not.

Declared in rendering order, so ``tuple(DayPart)`` is the order a grid is
laid out in and no caller sorts.

sport.description: Which sport this deal is for

DealDeckRequest.title: DealDeckRequest
DealDeckRequest.description:
What a deal is asked for. **One field, and that is the whole contract.**

**There is no `mode` here and there never will be.** The deck reads your own
declared Play intent for this sport, resolved backend-side, and *no
preference* is a working deck rather than a blocked one — indecision is not a
state this product refuses. A mode on this body would be the field the
telemetry constraint refuses: `mode` is null exactly when the surface is the
deck.

**There is no widening here either.** The relaxation ladder does not reach
the deck, so a deal carries no rung offers and there is no offer for one to
cite.

**There is nothing about a pass.** The suppression window crosses the wire in
no shape at all — no field, no code, no timestamp — which is what makes a
pass unable to become something stronger by way of a request.

km.title: Km
km.description: Whole kilometres between the two areas

area_code.title: Area Code
area_code.description: The candidate's coarse area, as a machine code

outside_their_radius.title: Outside Their Radius
outside_their_radius.description: Whether the searcher sits outside the candidate's own ring

DistanceEvidence.title: DistanceEvidence
DistanceEvidence.description:
How far away they are, and whether the searcher is outside *their* ring.

A candidate's own radius is a Liveness dock and **never a gate**: somebody
who set a small radius is not refusing to be found, and the searcher is
shown the fact rather than having the person removed. The standalone flat
dock for it is struck — the reciprocal reading already prices it, and
proportionately.

ErrorResponse.description: The body of every error response, on both API surfaces.

code.description: Stable, machine-readable identifier for this exact failure. The only half of the envelope a client may branch on.
code.title: Code

message.description: Human-readable diagnostic. Never the copy shown to a user — that is the client's, chosen from the code.
message.title: Message

trace_id.description: This request's identifier, also returned on the X-Request-ID header. Ties a client-side failure to a server log without logging a payload.
trace_id.title: Trace Id

details.description: Structured context for this code, when the code defines any.
details.title: Details

ErrorResponse.title: ErrorResponse

sport.description: Which sport this yes is for

player_id.title: Player Id
player_id.description: Who you would like to play

search_id.title: Search Id
search_id.description: The search this person was shown to you in. **Required** — a yes with no origin is refused rather than recorded with a null link.

ExpressInterestRequest.title: ExpressInterestRequest
ExpressInterestRequest.description:
One tap. **Three fields, and the third is not optional.**

``search_id`` is the **origin key**: it says which search surfaced this
person, and an interest citing a search that is unknown, that belongs to
somebody else or that never showed them is **refused, never linked as null**.
A silently dropped link is a denominator that lies, and *interests per search*
is how this engine is judged.

**The position is not sent.** The backend reads it off the cited search's own
returned rows, so the origin key is true by construction rather than by a
client being honest about where it was scrolled to.

mutual.title: Mutual
mutual.description: `true` when they had already said *Let's play* to you for this sport. **A mutual is told to both sides.** A one-sided yes is told to nobody, ever.

outstanding.description: Where this sport now stands against its cap, after this tap.

ExpressedInterestResponse.title: ExpressedInterestResponse
ExpressedInterestResponse.description:
What one tap answers with.

``mutual`` is the one thing this tells you about the other person, and you
have earned it by them having said yes to you first. Nobody is notified of a
one-sided yes, in either direction.

FactorResponse.title: FactorResponse
FactorResponse.description:
One evidence category's row: what it says, and which way it pulled.

``direction`` is one of ``up`` / ``down`` / ``neutral``, computed by the
engine from that category's own evidence against the final estimate. The
client never derives it — a client-side arrow is a second opinion about the
arithmetic, and two clients would eventually hold two of them.

sport.description: Which sport this four would play

mode.description: Competitive or for fun — the vector this reads under

search_id.title: Search Id
search_id.description: The search these people came off. **Required** — a forecast about somebody no search of yours showed is refused, not computed.

players.title: Players
players.description:
The people beside you, **in seat order**: the first is your partner in the arrangement the response marks `is_current`. One, two or three — a seat may be empty, and the forecast comes back **provisional** when one is.

Nobody twice, and never more than the sport seats. An empty seat is read *as if the missing player matched the one already there*, which is a claim about somebody who is not there — sending the same person twice would make that assumption look like a fact.

ForecastRequest.title: ForecastRequest
ForecastRequest.description:
What a four you composed yourself would leave on court.

**This route creates no search and records nothing.** Re-posting `/lineups`
per swap would enter a six-edit builder session into *searches run* as six
searches, which is a lie in the one table the product uses to judge itself.

`search_id` is **required**, and every player named must have appeared in
that search's returned rows. Unbounded, this would be a level lookup for any
player in the city reachable by id; bounded, it tells you nothing the
shortlist did not already show you.

ForecastResponse.title: ForecastResponse
ForecastResponse.description:
Three arrangements of a four you composed. **And no `search_id`.**

Nothing was searched and nothing was recorded, so there is no id to read this
back by and no breakdown to open. The two version stamps cross because a
forecast nobody can reproduce is a number nobody should trust.

sigma_group.title: Sigma Group
sigma_group.description: The confidence is part of the claim, so it crosses with it

assumption.title: Assumption
assumption.description: What the provisional figure assumed, as a code the client renders in its own words. Null when nothing was assumed.

ForecastSchema.title: ForecastSchema
ForecastSchema.description:
How even a game is forecast to be. One type, everywhere it appears.

``provisional`` travels **inside** the forecast rather than beside it: the
failure being guarded against is a screen showing the number without its
caveat, and a sibling boolean is exactly how the two get separated in a
refactor.

Gender.title: Gender
Gender.description:
What a player says about themselves — self-declared, freely changed.

Per person and never per sport, which is what keeps it on ``PlayerProfile``
rather than beside a rating (ADR-0089's cardinality, unchanged).

This is **a statement about which searches a player wishes to appear in**,
not a ruling by the platform on who anybody is. A player whose identity is
not on this list picks the answer that puts them where they want to be seen,
or takes ``PREFER_NOT_TO_SAY`` and appears in unconstrained searches only.
The platform adjudicates nothing.

GenderPreference.title: GenderPreference
GenderPreference.description:
Who a player is willing to be matched with — durable, not per search.

**Durable rather than per-search because the gate is mutual.** It has to be
evaluated against a player when somebody *else* searches and they are not
present, and a per-search setting cannot bind that direction at all. A
per-search override may **narrow** this, never widen past it.

GroupReason.title: GroupReason
GroupReason.description:
Why this four beat the runner-up. **One closed code, never a number.**

``G`` chose these four over the other combinations and the third refusal —
*never a number it cannot explain in one sentence with the evidence named* —
applies. A second score the player must trust is worse than none: it competes
with Fit and nobody can act on it. So the evidence half is paid here, by the
term with the largest margin between the winning combination and the
runner-up — the group analogue of the card's top three reasons
(``docs/adr/0117``).

Closed vocabulary and ``docs/adr/0106``-shaped: **the client writes the
sentence, the engine names which.**

InProgressAssessmentResponse.title: InProgressAssessmentResponse
InProgressAssessmentResponse.description:
One unfinished run: which assessment, and which sport it is for.

Carries no question, no result and no progress. A caller reading this is
deciding *where to send the player*; it re-reads the run it routes to, and
that read is the one that reproduces the outstanding question.

InProgressAssessmentsResponse.title: InProgressAssessmentsResponse
InProgressAssessmentsResponse.description:
Every unfinished run this player holds — empty when they hold none.

Empty is the ordinary answer for a new account and for a player who has
finished everything they started, so it is a 200 with an empty list rather
than a 404 or the singular form's 204.

Ordered by the sport registry, so a caller that wants one run can take the
first entry.

their_intent.description: The candidate's declaration for this sport

aligned.title: Aligned
aligned.description: Whether the two read the same evening

IntentAlignmentEvidence.title: IntentAlignmentEvidence
IntentAlignmentEvidence.description:
What kind of evening each of them is after.

**Intent is a weight and not a gate.** A candidate who declared the opposite
loses the term's entire weight and takes no further charge — the zero is the
whole answer, and a second dock would be a gate wearing a modifier's clothes.
A candidate who has *not* declared has the term dropped and renormalised away
instead, so declaring against the searcher already costs strictly more than
saying nothing.

outgoing.title: Outgoing
outgoing.description: Yeses you sent that are still in flight, newest first. Every one carries its own `expires_at`.

mutual.title: Mutual
mutual.description: Yeses you sent that came back. **Both of you said it**, which is the only way somebody else's yes reaches you at all.

outstanding.title: Outstanding
outstanding.description: One entry per sport, always — the count and the cap in force. Sent before you are near the limit, on purpose.

InterestListResponse.title: InterestListResponse
InterestListResponse.description:
Your own *Let's play* screen. **Outgoing and mutuals only.**

There is no incoming list and there will not be one: a yes nobody has
answered stays silent, which is what makes saying yes low-stakes. The two
lists are disjoint — a yes that came back is in `mutual` and not in
`outgoing` — so a client renders both without deriving either.

LevelDirection.title: LevelDirection
LevelDirection.description:
Which side of the searcher a candidate's Level sits on.

A code and not a sign on ``delta``, because the client's sentence differs in
all three cases and a renderer deriving *"above"* from a sign is the display
logic the presentation boundary exists to keep out.

It lives here rather than beside the wire shape for the reason
``EvidenceKind`` does: the engine computes it and the schema publishes it, so
a second spelling on the schema's side would be two answers to *which way is
up*. A module may import an engine; the reverse is the fence.

LevelFitEvidence.title: LevelFitEvidence
LevelFitEvidence.description:
How far apart the two levels are, and which way.

The tolerance behind the curve is absolute on μ and never reads a band: the
shipped bands are deliberately uneven because *evidence* is unevenly
available down the scale, not because a tenth of a point means less at the
top.

candidates.title: Candidates
candidates.description:
Ranked. **An empty list is a `200`** — the honest empty state is an answer, not a failure.

A read-back may carry withheld rows: the record is immutable and the gates are live, so a row the product has since agreed not to show keeps its place and states that it is withheld. Branch on `withheld` — a fresh search never carries one.

LineupResponse.title: LineupResponse
LineupResponse.description:
The shortlist's envelope, its rows, and the court they were seated on.

One envelope and one row shape across every surface, so the read-back has one
renderer to reproduce: what a line-up adds is the seating, not a second way
of describing a person.

seats.title: Seats
seats.description: The court as it currently stands, seat by seat, in the arrangement marked `is_current`.

arrangements.title: Arrangements
arrangements.description: Every way round, each with its own forecast. Empty only when nobody could be seated at all.

group_reason.description: Why this four beat the runner-up, as one closed code the client writes the sentence for. **Omitted when there was no runner-up** — one admissible four is not a four that won an argument.

dock.description: `NO_SHARED_SLOTS` when the four of you have no hour in common. **A dock, never a refusal**: nobody is removed from the court for it, and the honest line is that you would all have to bend.

LineupSchema.title: LineupSchema
LineupSchema.description:
The court, every way round it can sit, and one reason it won.

**A partial line-up is this shape with fewer people in it** — never a
different one, and never an error. *Nobody* is this shape with every seat
carrying a reason, so a client renders one thing.

player_id.title: Player Id
player_id.description: Who is in this seat, to look up in `candidates[]`. **Omitted on an open seat**, and on your own — you are not a row of your own search.

unfilled_reason.description:
Why this seat is empty. **A seat is never filled below the quality floor to complete a four**, a newcomer least of all — *three of four* is an honest answer, and so is nobody.

`NO_ADMISSIBLE_COMBINATION` is the one worth reading twice: there were people, and no four of you could share a court. Omitted on a seat that is taken.

LineupSeatSchema.title: LineupSeatSchema
LineupSeatSchema.description:
One place on the court, with the person in it or the reason it is empty.

**The person is named by id and their breakdown rides once**, in
`candidates[]` — the same list every other surface returns, carrying **the
same number the shortlist showed**, because nothing is re-scored behind your
back when somebody sits down. Four breakdowns repeated across a court and
three arrangements is four chances for two copies to disagree, on a payload
that is already tens of kilobytes.

LivenessReason.title: LivenessReason
LivenessReason.description:
Why somebody moved, as a code. **Never as a number.**

Ten values: the eight printable signals, with the full inbox spelled as its
three coarse rungs instead of its own name. Their inbox depth is theirs — the
rung crosses and the count does not — and each rung names its own code, so a
threshold moving does not silently re-point a code at a different depth.

The two **silent** signals are absent by construction rather than by
omission: a silent move carries points and no code, so there is no name on
the value to print. ``tests/unit/test_matchmaking_shortlist_contract.py``
holds this enum to exactly the printable roster.

LocationAreaResource.title: LocationAreaResource
LocationAreaResource.description:
Where a player plays.

**What is sent and what is kept are not the same number.** A client sends the
fix its device gave it; the platform rounds to roughly a kilometre before
anything is recorded, and it is the rounded pair that comes back here. The
precise fix is never stored and never shareable
(``../../../../CONTEXT.md`` — *Location area*).

ModifierCode.title: ModifierCode
ModifierCode.description:
The three modifiers inside the budget, and the dock outside it.

Every one of them **prints**: a modifier that could move a score without
owing a sentence would be Liveness wearing stage 4's clothes, and Liveness
has a budget for exactly that.

ModifierSchema.title: ModifierSchema
ModifierSchema.description: One modifier that fired, and what it was worth on this pairing.

OptimisedFor.title: OptimisedFor
OptimisedFor.description:
Whom this search was run for.

``GROUP`` exists because a line-up with seats locked is no longer optimising
for the searcher, who may end up with a worse individual match than an empty
builder would have given them — and the screen has to say so. A shortlist is
always ``SEARCHER``, and the field is on the envelope rather than implied by
the surface so that one renderer reads one fact.

expires_at.title: Expires At
expires_at.description: When this yes lapses. **Dated when it was created** and never extended by tapping again — a second tap changes nothing. On expiry the row is simply gone: there is no *expired* state and no archive.

OutgoingInterestSchema.title: OutgoingInterestSchema
OutgoingInterestSchema.description:
One yes you sent, and when it lapses.

``expires_at`` is on the row from the moment it was created, and the client
**renders** it rather than computing it: the TTL behind it is ruleset
configuration and never crosses as a number.

cap.title: Cap
cap.description: The most you may have in flight for this sport at once. **Read it from here, never hardcode it** — it is ruleset configuration and may move between releases.

OutstandingSchema.title: OutstandingSchema
OutstandingSchema.description:
How many yeses you have in flight for one sport, and the cap in force.

**Outstanding means sent, unexpired and not yet mutual** — a mutual has been
answered and is no longer in flight. The pair travels together on every read,
because a cap you cannot see is a refusal you cannot predict.

photo_id.title: Photo Id
photo_id.description: Permanent id — what the profile commit carries

url.title: Url
url.description: Short-lived signed URL that reads this photo. Not a stable address: it is signed for one player, for one window, and there is no public bucket behind it.

expires_at.title: Expires At
expires_at.description: When the URL stops working. Ask for the photo again to get another; there is no way to extend one.

review.description:
What the on-court check concluded about this photo, or `null` where this response carries no verdict.

**`null` is not `allowed`.** The upload always answers with one of the two values; the read never carries one. A client that has not been told anything must warn about nothing.

**A warning and nothing else.** `flagged` does not refuse, delete or hold back a photo: it is stored, it keeps its id, and a profile commit takes it like any other. The check is wrong sometimes, and the cost of being wrong is a sentence rather than a signup.

A code, not copy — the words belong to the client.

PhotoResponse.title: PhotoResponse
PhotoResponse.description:
One photo: the id a profile commit will carry, and a URL that reads it.

The same shape from the upload and from the read, so a client renders a tile
it has just filled and a tile it is restoring with one code path.

**The URL is not an identifier and must not be stored as one.** It carries a
signature and stops working at ``expires_at``; the id is what is permanent.

## The verdict crosses; the evidence does not

``review`` is the on-court check's conclusion and it is a **code**, never a
sentence: the backend emits codes and the client owns the words
(``docs/adr/0022``). ``review-note`` — the model, the prompt-set fingerprint
and the raw similarity vector — stays on the object. It is evidence for us
rather than a fact about the player, and a confidence score on the wire is an
invitation to a client that renders one.

**The upload carries it and the read does not**, which is why the field is
optional and why ``null`` is not ``allowed``. Two reasons, and neither is
that the read is harder. A warning belongs to the moment a player *chose* a
photograph; a tile being restored is a photograph they already kept, and
saying it again is a screen re-litigating a decision the player made. And the
read would have to pay for it: ``GET /photos/{id}`` proves existence and signs
a URL, and no part of it looks at what the store holds beside the bytes — the
verdict is user metadata, which every S3-compatible store answers with a
request per object. So the shape stays one shape and the tile stays one code
path, exactly as the paragraph above promises; what differs is whether this
response has anything to say about the check.

PhotoReviewDecision.title: PhotoReviewDecision
PhotoReviewDecision.description:
What the review port concluded about an image.

Two values, and there is deliberately no ``REJECTED``. The on-court check
**soft-warns rather than hard-blocks** (``docs/adr/0091``): a false reject
stops a real player on their first day, and that cost does not fall now that
the other side of the trade has got heavier. Adding a blocking value later is
an addition; shipping one now would be a behaviour nothing has earned.

There is also no value for *the reviewer could not be asked*. This enum says
what the reviewer **concluded** about an image, and an outage is not a
conclusion about an image — see `verdict_when_unreviewable`.

PlayIntent.title: PlayIntent
PlayIntent.description:
What kind of game a player wants, in one sport.

Declared per ``(player, sport)`` — see ``play_intent_declaration.py`` for
why that is its own aggregate rather than a field on the profile.

nickname.title: Nickname
nickname.description: The whole handle. There is no name in this platform and **nothing may derive a familiar form from it** — every sentence naming somebody uses the whole handle or names nobody.

photo_id.title: Photo Id
photo_id.description: The first photo — order is meaning in a photo list. **An id, never a URL**: a presigned link cannot live in a record kept forever, so the link is minted per response. **Omitted** when the player has no photo, and the client draws the generated court poster.

area_code.title: Area Code
area_code.description: Their coarse area, as a machine code

social_tags.title: Social Tags
social_tags.description: The Social tag ids they hold

level.title: Level
level.description: Their Level, as RacketSkill published it

counted_games.title: Counted Games
counted_games.description: How many counted games they have played. **Omitted today**: the games ledger has no provider in this build, and a zero would be an invented one rather than a measured nothing.

PlayerCardSchema.title: PlayerCardSchema
PlayerCardSchema.description:
Who this person is, on a card. **A closed list with two permanent gaps.**

No bio and no free text of any kind, ever; and **no activity recency at any
granularity** — not a timestamp, not *active today*, not a green dot.
Liveness reaches a screen the one way it is sanctioned to: as a reason code.

PlayerProfileOptionsResponse.title: PlayerProfileOptionsResponse
PlayerProfileOptionsResponse.description:
Everything a client needs to *render* the profile steps, in one round trip.

A handful of facts rather than one endpoint each, because they are the same
kind of thing — closed, read-only, and needed by the same part of onboarding
at the same moment.

**Fields are only ever added.** A shipped mobile app parses this document for
months after it stops being built, so a new field goes on the end and the
ones already here keep their names and their types.

PlayerProfileResponse.title: PlayerProfileResponse
PlayerProfileResponse.description:
A player's profile as it now stands.

The same body whether the commit created the profile or replayed an earlier
one, so a client that only wants its profile needs no branch on the status.

**No gender value comes back out**, and that is a rule rather than an
oversight (``docs/adr/0096`` §6): a preference crosses the wire *in*, on a
search; no response shape carries a gender out and no card renders one.
This body is only ever the caller's own profile, so nothing here would leak
a third party's answer — the field is left off anyway, because the moment
one response shape carries it, *which* shapes may is a judgement call made
per endpoint instead of a line nobody has to re-argue. Nothing reads it back
today: onboarding sends it once, and there is no profile editor. When one
exists, adding it here is an addition to this document and ADR-0096's
ticket's to make.

**Fields are only ever added.** A shipped mobile app parses this document for
months after it stops being built.

matched.title: Matched
matched.description: Tag ids they both hold, in this column

PlayingStyleEvidence.title: PlayingStyleEvidence
PlayingStyleEvidence.description:
What the two of them are like during the hour on court.

The split from social vibe is **by relationship, not by tag group**: every
matrix row carries its own column, so a tag can be read for the hour on court
in one row and for the evening around it in another.

A pair with nothing firing is *different, not incompatible* — the term's zero
is a real clash, never an absence of relationship.

radius_km_used.title: Radius Km Used
radius_km_used.description: The searcher's own radius, in whole kilometres

players_in_range.title: Players In Range
players_in_range.description: How many candidates cleared every gate. **Post-gate, always** — a pre-gate count beside this one would be the delta a mutual preference hid, per searcher.

window.description: When a game found on this grid would plausibly be played, as a code. Derived by the backend from the grid the search ran on; there is no window picker anywhere.

post_gate.title: Post Gate
post_gate.description: Always true. It travels so the count cannot be misread.

PoolSchema.title: PoolSchema
PoolSchema.description:
What the searcher is told about the pool this answer came from.

Sent on **every** search and not only on empty ones: a thin pool and a broken
floor are indistinguishable without it.

confidence.title: Confidence
confidence.description: The platform's confidence transform over the combined σ, as a whole percent. Never 100: the platform cannot tell a player it is certain.

PredictedBalanceEvidence.title: PredictedBalanceEvidence
PredictedBalanceEvidence.description:
How even the game is forecast to be, and how sure of that the platform is.

``pct`` is the forecast the player is shown; ``confidence`` is the platform's
existing σ transform and never a second spelling of certainty.

Prompt.title: Prompt
Prompt.description:
What the app is offering to ask. **Codes, never sentences.**

The kernel's rule reaches the matcher unchanged (``docs/adr/0022``): the
backend emits a code and the client writes the words. *"Keep 15 km?"* is one
phrasing of ``KEEP_THIS_RADIUS`` in one language, and a backend that shipped
it would own the copy for every client that ever exists.

slots.title: Slots
slots.description: The week this search actually ran on, as codes

mode.description: The mode your recent searches keep choosing

PromptSchema.title: PromptSchema
PromptSchema.description:
A question the app is offering to ask. **It never changes a value.**

The platform notices that you improvised a week, that you keep widening to
the same radius, that your searches disagree with what you declared, or that
the week on your profile is months old — and in every case it asks. The
payload is the value already in play, so the sheet can show the change rather
than describe it.

accepted.title: Accepted
accepted.description: The player's answer. `null` means the question was not answered, which is refused — it is never read as `false`.

copy_version.title: Copy Version
copy_version.description: Identifier of the exact copy the player was shown. Not the copy itself — the words are the client's and are never stored here.

ProposalsOptInRequest.title: ProposalsOptInRequest
ProposalsOptInRequest.description:
The answer to the proposals question, and the words it was given against.

``accepted`` is **nullable and required**, which is the shape of a question
that has no default. Null means *not answered* and is refused by the commit
with ``proposals_opt_in_not_answered``; it is not a quiet ``false``, because
a recorded refusal and an unanswered question are different facts and only
one of them is consent (``../../../../CONTEXT.md`` — *Skipping is not
consent*).

``copy_version`` identifies the exact wording the player was shown. It is
required because consent gathered against one sentence is not consent to a
different one, and a consent record that cannot name its words cannot
evidence anything.

copy_version.title: Copy Version
copy_version.description: The copy this answer was given against

ProposalsOptInResponse.title: ProposalsOptInResponse
ProposalsOptInResponse.description:
The standing answer, and the evidence recorded with it.

This is the *current* answer. The **history** — every answer this player ever
gave, against which words and on which surface — is the stream, and nothing
serves it yet because nothing has asked for it.

QuestionResponse.title: QuestionResponse
QuestionResponse.description: A question in reading order: category, situation, question, answers.

RatingResponse.title: RatingResponse
RatingResponse.description:
One sport's Skill rating.

``mu`` and ``sigma`` are the Level and the Uncertainty — the same spelling
``ResultResponse`` already puts on the wire for the same two numbers, so a
client never has to learn that the rating it was just shown and the rating it
later reads back are described in two vocabularies.

RatingsResponse.title: RatingsResponse
RatingsResponse.description: Every sport this player is rated at — empty when they are rated at none.

sport.description: Which sport this card was for

player_id.title: Player Id
player_id.description: Whose card you are passing on

search_id.title: Search Id
search_id.description: The deal this person was dealt to you in. **Required** — a pass with no origin is refused rather than recorded with a null link.

RecordPassRequest.title: RecordPassRequest
RecordPassRequest.description:
One *not today*, and where the card came from. **Write-only.**

Nothing is returned by this route and no route anywhere returns a pass — not
to you, not as a count, not as *"you have passed on twelve people"*.

`search_id` is the **Origin key** and is required, exactly as it is for a
yes: a pass citing a search that is unknown, that belongs to somebody else or
that never showed that person is refused rather than recorded with an empty
link. **The position is not sent** — the backend reads it off the cited
search's own rows.

**How long it lasts is not yours to name**, and there is no field here for
it. A pass keeps somebody out of *your deck* only, for a window this backend
decides; it never reaches a shortlist, a line-up or a forecast, it never
touches their deck, and a second pass buys exactly the same window and no
more. The control that removes a person from a person is a **block**, and it
is deliberately a heavier gesture.

Relationship.title: Relationship
Relationship.description:
What one seat is to the searcher. **Stated, never inferred from a side.**

``the-two-contracts.md`` §5: the whole partner/opponent asymmetry hangs on
it, and a client deriving it from which side somebody sits on would be a
second implementation of a domain rule.

RelaxationAsk.title: RelaxationAsk
RelaxationAsk.description:
Which of the searcher's own asks a rung relaxes.

The vocabulary is closed at two because there are exactly two asks a searcher
makes: when they can play, and how far they will go. A third value would be
the engine relaxing something the player never asked for, which is the line
``docs/adr/0099`` draws.

strands.title: Strands
strands.description: The strands that produced a reading, over the closed six

floor_breached.title: Floor Breached
floor_breached.description: Whether the published score sits under the reliability bar

ReliabilityEvidence.title: ReliabilityEvidence
ReliabilityEvidence.description:
What the candidate's record says about turning up and following through.

``score`` is the **published Player Score** — the number on the player's own
profile — and never the matcher's private per-mode blend of the same six
strands. A penalty justified by a figure that exists nowhere a human can look
is unexplainable, and a player who works their visible score back up must be
able to see the penalty lift.

ReliabilityStrand.title: ReliabilityStrand
ReliabilityStrand.description:
The six strands a reliability reading is built from, read separately.

They are weighted **per mode** and the two vectors order people oppositely —
a candidate strong on *confirms results* and weak on *sportsmanship* wins in
competitive and loses in for fun. A single blended score cannot express that,
which is the whole argument for the decomposition, and it is justified for
exactly as long as such a pair exists (``ranking-weights.md`` §6).

**Three different blends of these six exist in this system and confusing them
is a live risk:** the published Player Score at 35/20/15/12/10/8, and these
two. The reliability *floor* reads the published one — the one deliberate
exception, because a penalty justified by a figure that exists nowhere a
human can look is unexplainable.

confidence_ceiling.title: Confidence Ceiling
confidence_ceiling.description: The highest `confidence` this engine version can reach, as a whole percent — a questionnaire has an irreducible limit, so a rating at this value was held by the ceiling and one below it by its own evidence. Absent only for a rating replayed from an engine version that has since been retired, which is the same case that carries no `confidence_reason`: such a rating keeps its numbers and loses its explanation. Do not hold a local copy of this number — it is version-scoped and may be retuned without a client release.

sport.description: Which sport this line-up is for

mode.description: Competitive or for fun — the weight vector for this one search. It selects the **group** vector too, which inverts against the shortlist's: for fun puts more weight on how the four get on than on how even the sides are.

locked_seats.title: Locked Seats
locked_seats.description:
Players you have already seated by hand, **in seat order**. Send none and the engine fills every seat; send one or two and it fills the rest **around them**, which is when it starts optimising for the group rather than for you — `search.optimised_for` says so.

Everybody named must be somebody this search can still seat, and they must be able to share a court **with each other** — every gate binds all six pairs. Either refusal is `locked_seat_not_available`, naming nobody, rather than a quiet replacement.

Nobody twice, and never more than the sport seats.

availability_override.title: Availability Override
availability_override.description: The week to run **this one line-up** against. Omit to use the grid on your profile — **omit it, never send `null`**.

offered_by_search_id.title: Offered By Search Id
offered_by_search_id.description: The search whose relaxation offer this one accepts. Taking a rung is a **new search citing the one that offered it**.

rung.description: Which rung of that search's offer you are taking. Sent with `offered_by_search_id` or not at all.

RunLineupRequest.title: RunLineupRequest
RunLineupRequest.description:
⚡ *Fill the seats.* **The line-up and fill-seats are one request.**

They differ by `locked_seats` being non-empty, which is a property of what
you send rather than of where you send it — so hand-seating somebody and
pressing ⚡ is the same shape as ⚡ on an empty court, and there is no second
route for a client to get wrong.

There is **no seat count** here and there never will be: how many people sit
down is the sport's own fact. There is no radius either, for the reason the
shortlist has none.

sport.description: Which sport this search is for

mode.description: Competitive or for fun — the weight vector for this one search, and nothing else. Two values, where a Play intent has three.

availability_override.title: Availability Override
availability_override.description:
The week to run **this one search** against, when the player edited it on the search screen. Omit to use the grid on your profile — **omit it, never send `null`**.

**It is an ask and never a correction.** Nothing here writes your profile; the app offers to save it afterwards.

offered_by_search_id.title: Offered By Search Id
offered_by_search_id.description: The search whose relaxation offer this one accepts. **Taking a rung is a new search citing the one that offered it**, never a silent change to your saved preferences.

rung.description: Which rung of that search's offer you are taking. Sent with `offered_by_search_id` or not at all — and the widening itself is **not** sent: the backend reads it off the offer it made.

RunSearchRequest.title: RunSearchRequest
RunSearchRequest.description:
What a client may send. **Asks only, never a fact about the searcher.**

There is deliberately **no radius here, and there never will be.** The
searcher's ask *is* their profile radius, read at request time; widening
happens only by taking a rung offer. A radius supplied by a phone is a gate
evaluated on a lie, and this is the field it would arrive through.

Rung.title: Rung
Rung.description:
Which rung of the ladder an offer is.

Three values and no more. They are letters rather than numbers because
``docs/adr/0099`` rebuilt the ladder from scratch and a rung ``1`` would
invite a reader to line it up against §9.8's struck rung 1, which relaxed
something else entirely.

rung.description: Which rung. The list is in the engine's recommended order — times first, because a slot you were already free in costs nothing where distance costs travel on every game forever — but the order is a recommendation and any rung may be taken directly.

ask.description: Which of **your own** asks it relaxes. A rung never touches a measurement, a term, a weight, or the quality floor.

candidates_above_floor.title: Candidates Above Floor
candidates_above_floor.description: How many people would clear the quality floor at this rung, from a genuine re-run. The number on the button is true.

window.description: This rung's **own** window. A challenge sliding from `WEEKEND` to `THIS_WEEK` is part of what widening costs, and you see it before you pay it.

radius_km.title: Radius Km
radius_km.description: The widened radius, on a `RADIUS` rung. Always inside the same 1-50 km your own slider holds: a relaxation never offers a radius you could not have set yourself, so a searcher already at 50 km is offered no radius rung at all.

slot.title: Slot
slot.description: The one cell this rung would add to your week, on a `TIMES` rung, as `day:PART`. For this search only.

RungOfferSchema.title: RungOfferSchema
RungOfferSchema.description:
One rung of the relaxation ladder, priced. **Offered, never applied.**
